title: Primates Also Become Germophobes After Living Through a Viral Outbreak - Nautilus
gist: A Royal Society Open Science study of Japanese macaques at a Texas sanctuary hit by simian retrovirus Type II in 2020 suggests primates also adopt avoidance behaviors after a viral outbreak, possibly shedding light on the evolutionary origins of disgust. The article gives only the setup, not the findings.

insights.claim: In 2020 simian retrovirus Type II, which causes AIDS-like immune deficiency, swept three of four groups of Japanese macaques at a Texas primate sanctuary, creating a natural experiment comparing exposed and unexposed groups.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Outbreak-behavior research is a source of natural experiments on disease avoidance.

insights.claim: Humans are not the only primates that take extreme precautions during viral outbreaks, according to the study in Royal Society Open Science.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Supports an evolutionary basis for pandemic-era hygiene behavior.
insights.locator: According to a new study published in Royal Society Open Science

insights.claim: Primate behavioral responses to outbreaks could shed light on the evolutionary origins of disgust.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Background for behavioral-response models of disease.
insights.locator: And it could shed light on the evolutionary origins of disgust
